question: Vienna, 1846. Mothers die of fever far more often in one clinic than in the one next door. What is killing them?
answer: The doctors' hands. Ignaz Semmelweis struck off every rival he could test: the air, the crowding, the priest's bell. What was left was the one difference between the clinics: the doctors came from dissecting corpses, the midwives did not. From May 1847 they washed in chlorine; deaths fell to 13 in 1,000.
move: Strike off every suspect you can test; the one left standing is your lead.
ask: When something goes wrong at home or at work, do I test the rival explanations, or chase the most vivid one?

clues.text: In the doctors' clinic about 1 mother in 10 dies; next door, with midwives, 1 in 30.
Both clinics share one building, one city's air, and take mothers on alternate days.
The midwives' clinic is the more crowded: women beg to be sent there.
The priest stops ringing his bell through the doctors' wards. Deaths don't fall.
A doctor cut by a student's scalpel during an autopsy dies of the same fever.

scene.why: The silent bell struck off the last rival. One difference was left: the doctors came from corpses.

source: Semmelweis, The Etiology of Childbed Fever; Loudon, James Lind Library, 2013
